DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Pricing Proposal, Weekend Rate Restructure (Harbourside Hotel)

## What the proposal says

From 1 June, the proposal raises the weekend Best Available Rate (BAR) from £145 to £165 and adds a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday. It rests on three arguments:
- weekend occupancy rose after last June's £10 increase;
- value-for-money scores are strong;
- the hotel is priced £20–35 below its competitive set.

It projects at least £204,000 a year in extra revenue, calling that figure a floor.

## Verdict

There is a real case for a higher weekend rate. The gap to competitors is genuine, and 31 Saturdays sold out last year. But the evidence and the revenue figure don't hold up against the proposal's own data:

1. **The "price sensitivity test" is the seasonal peak.** Occupancy rose in July because July is the festival and school-holiday month, as §2 itself says.
2. **The revenue figure uses 124 rooms**, but the hotel has 112.
3. **The £20 increase is applied to every weekend room-night**, including corporate and group business that will stay on contracted rates.
4. **The two-night minimum conflicts with the hotel's largest Saturday segment.** Wedding guests (38% of Saturday bookings) stay one night.

The £204,000 is not a floor. It is closer to a ceiling.

## Arithmetic

| Item | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Average weekend occupancy | Mean of the 12 monthly figures | 79.2% ✓ |
| Gap to competitors | £165–180 against £145 | £20–35 ✓ |
| Revenue at 124 rooms | 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 | £203,800 ✓ |
| **Revenue at 112 rooms** | **112 × 104 × 79% × £20** | **£184,000** |
| Size of the increase | £145 → £165 | +14%, twice last year's 7% |

## 1. The June-to-July rise is seasonal, not a test of price sensitivity

The £10 increase took effect in the last week of June. July occupancy (89%) was higher than June's (81%). But §2 describes July and August as the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. Occupancy would almost certainly have risen anyway, so the comparison tells us nothing about how guests respond to price. The author's note calls it "a direct test"; it isn't one.

Two comparisons would give real evidence:
- **July 2025 against July 2024**, before and after the increase in the same month.
- **The change against the competitive set**, if competitor occupancy data is available. That would show whether Harbourside gained or lost share.

The value-for-money score of 8.4 is also weaker evidence than it appears. The hotel is the cheapest in its set, which probably explains part of the score, and a rate rise is likely to lower it. The score reflects the current price; it doesn't show tolerance for a higher one.

## 2. The revenue estimate overstates the gain

- **Room count.** §2 says 112 rooms; §5 calculates on 124. At 112 rooms, the figure is £184,000 before any other correction.
- **Not every room pays BAR.** Corporate and already-contracted group rates will be honoured (§6). Weddings make up 38% of Saturday bookings and are typically blocked through the couple, so likely at a group rate. The £20 increase applies only to BAR room-nights. For illustration only: if Friday were all BAR and Saturday 62% BAR, the gain would fall to about £150,000. The actual BAR share by night would settle the figure.
- **Commission.** Bookings through online travel agencies pay commission on the higher rate, so net revenue rises by less than £20 a room.
- **Bookings already made.** Weekend bookings for June and later summer made before 15 May stay at £145, which reduces the first-year gain further.
- **"Occupancy maintained" is not a conservative assumption.** A 14% rise moves the hotel from the cheapest in its set to level with the cheapest competitor. The prudent case includes some loss in occupancy. A sensitivity table at, say, 0, −3 and −5 points would show the realistic range.

## 3. The two-night minimum could lose revenue

- **Weddings.** Wedding guests make up 38% of Saturday bookings and stay Saturday to Sunday. Contracted blocks will be honoured, but future wedding blocks, and guests who book individually, would face a choice between paying for a second night or booking elsewhere. Quayside Hall's guests can easily stay at another nearby hotel.
- **Saturdays that don't sell out.** On roughly 21 Saturdays in 2025 the hotel did not sell out. On those nights, a minimum stay turns away one-night guests without a full house to replace them.
- **The extra revenue is assumed, not shown.** The proposal calls the extra Friday and Sunday nights "material" but doesn't quantify them. Some guests will extend their stay; others will go elsewhere. The net effect could be negative, so the author's note is wrong that the estimate leaves out only upside.

A narrower rule would capture most of the benefit with less risk:
- apply the minimum stay only on dates forecast to sell out, such as festival weekends and peak summer Saturdays;
- exempt wedding blocks.

## 4. Monitoring

- **The trigger compares only with last year.** Comparing month by month against 2025 can't separate the effect of the rate from changes in market demand. Comparing performance against the competitive set would isolate the rate effect.
- **The first months are the weakest test.** June to September are peak months, when demand is least sensitive to price. Effects on price sensitivity are most likely to show in the shoulder and winter months.
- **The trigger is coarse.** It needs a full month's data and then a five-point fall. Weekly pick-up against the same weeks last year would give an earlier warning, and some of that data is already collected for the monthly report.

## What holds

These parts of the proposal are sound:
- The occupancy average and the competitor rate gap, both from the proposal's own data.
- The pressure on Saturday inventory, with 31 sell-outs.
- The commitment to honour corporate and contracted group rates.
- Weekly pick-up monitoring.
- The underlying judgement that weekend rates have room to rise, especially at peak.

## Summary

**Settled now:**
- The June-to-July rise reflects seasonal demand, not price tolerance.
- The revenue calculation uses the wrong room count.
- The £20 gain applies only to BAR room-nights, not all room-nights.
- The two-night minimum works against the wedding segment.

**Still open, and what would settle each:**

| Question | How to settle it |
|---|---|
| How weekend guests respond to price | July 2025 against July 2024, and against the competitive set |
| What the rate rise is actually worth | BAR share by night, OTA commission, and an occupancy sensitivity range |
| Net effect of the minimum stay | Last year's Saturday one-night stays by segment, and their effect on Friday and Sunday nights |

**Recommendation:**
- Approve a weekend rate increase, considering a phased approach (for example £155 now, then a review) or higher rates on peak dates only.
- Restrict the two-night minimum to forecast sell-out dates, with wedding blocks exempt.
- Ask for the revenue estimate to be restated on 112 rooms and BAR-only room-nights, with a downside case.
